what: Tomoyasu Horikawa (NTT Communication Science Laboratories) published 'mind captioning': fMRI activity of people recalling videos from memory was decoded into semantic features and turned into free descriptive sentences of the recalled content.
fit: It writes out in sentences, by machine from brain activity alone, what a person is mentally picturing (recalled video content), not what they say or try to say; mechanism is fMRI decoding into language-model features with iterative text generation.

sources.title: Mind captioning: Evolving descriptive text of mental content from human brain activity
sources.quote: The method also generalized to verbalize recalled content, functioning as an interpretive interface between mental representations and text

sources.title: Mind captioning: Evolving descriptive text of mental content from human brain activity
sources.quote: generates descriptive text mirroring brain representations via semantic features computed by a deep language model

note: Replaces the 2020 UCSF result (Makin/Chang), which decodes overt speech from a 50-sentence set and is not thoughts. Rejected candidates: Dewan 1964 alpha-rhythm Morse code and the 1988 P300 speller (letter selection by voluntary attention/blinking, not decoding of thought); Horikawa et al. 2013 (Science) dream decoding and Horikawa & Kamitani 2017 imagined-object decoding (output is predicted object category labels from a fixed list, not text or images of the thoughts); Miyawaki 2008 and Nishimoto 2011 image/movie reconstruction (stimulus the person is seeing, per the test cases); Shen et al. 2019 imagery reconstruction (crude shapes, from fMRI, not text); Tang et al. 2023 (semantic decoder of perceived/imagined speech: speech, excluded by the test case); Moses 2021 and Willett 2021 (attempted speech/handwriting); Kunz 2025 inner speech (imagined speech). Mind captioning 2025 is the earliest I found that turns non-verbal mental content (recalled videos) into free text, and it still needs hours of fMRI training per person, so it is a partial fit; low confidence. Not verified as the first: later work could be argued either way.
searched: WebSearch for 'mind captioning' (Horikawa Science Advances 2025) and for Horikawa Kamitani 2013 dream decoding; fetched Crossref record and PMC article of the 2025 paper; Wikipedia BCI page; archive.org full text for 1960s alpha-rhythm devices (Dewan 1964); no ia_search hits for earlier thought-to-text machines. Considered the thinkwriter/dream-recorder aliases: no pre-2000 working system found.

concept_note: Second pass (2020 UCSF decoding of spoken sentences) rejected as speech decoding. Replaced by 2025 mind captioning (recalled video content to descriptive sentences), a partial fit at low confidence. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption: it is a lab method needing hours of per-person fMRI; no one uses it outside labs.

what: Edmond M. Dewan (US Air Force Cambridge Research Laboratories) demonstrated a device that detects the brain's alpha rhythm and let a person send Morse code to a machine by voluntarily switching the rhythm on and off.
fit: Scalp EEG signals are filtered and detected by a machine, and the person sends coded commands to it by voluntary brain activity alone, without moving a muscle.

sources.title: Air Force Research Review 1964-11: Vol 3 Iss 9
sources.quote: Dewan has successfully demonstrated his device to several doctors by operating it with his own alpha rhythm.

note: Replaces Lucier's Music for Solo Performer (1965): later than Dewan's 1964 report, and as an artwork it is borderline (alpha waves of the performer drive percussion via analog amplifiers; I accept it as a borderline BCI but it is not the earliest). Vidal 1973-77 (the 'BCI challenge', VEP cursor/maze) is later; Fetz 1969 monkeys and Grey Walter 1964 not verified or animal. Dewan's exact demonstration date is not given beyond the Nov 1964 report, so the year is the report's year or slightly earlier. Only one contemporary source; the Luce 1966 book 'Sleep' mentions Dewan's alpha filter but is a lending book that cannot be read.
searched: ia_search3 for 'alpha rhythm' Morse 1962-1970, Dewan alpha brain waves communicate 1960-1966, brain waves control electroencephalograph 1940-1963; Wikipedia BCI and Alvin Lucier pages; archive.org Electronic Music Review 1967 for Lucier.

what: Philip Kennedy and Roy Bakay implanted a neurotrophic-cone electrode in the motor cortex of the locked-in patient Johnny Ray, who learned to control a computer cursor to communicate.
fit: A paralyzed person used signals from his own brain, via an implanted electrode, to control a computer, for the real purpose of communicating when he could not move.

sources.title: Restoration of neural output from a paralyzed patient by a direct brain connection
sources.quote: Restoration of neural output from a paralyzed patient by a direct brain connection

note: Kept the second pass. Considered Birbaumer's EEG thought translation device (reported in Nature 1999, patient training from 1990s, later than the 1998 implant report) and the Farwell-Donchin P300 speller (1988, tested on healthy subjects, lab only); Dewan 1964 and Vidal 1977 were lab demonstrations. The cursor use by Johnny Ray is dated by the implant year; the Crossref record only gives the title and publication month, so the title quote supports the event and the Wikipedia quote the year.
searched: Wikipedia BCI page; Crossref for Kennedy and Bakay 1998 (NeuroReport) and Birbaumer 1999 (Nature 'A spelling device for the paralysed', record date 1999-03).

concept_note: Demonstration moved from Lucier 1965 to Dewan's 1964 alpha-rhythm Morse-code device (earlier and a more direct machine-control fit); Lucier's piece is borderline and later. Practical use kept at 1998 (Johnny Ray). No mass_adoption: implanted and EEG BCIs remain clinical or research tools.

what: Ivan Sutherland and students built a head-mounted display whose computer generated a stereo perspective view that changed as the wearer moved his head (running on a PDP-1 at Harvard in August 1968).
fit: A computer draws a three-dimensional world in each eye and updates it from head tracking so the user sees it as if it were around him, though only as crude wireframe lines.

sources.publisher: Harvard University / ARPA report (Computer History Museum archive)
sources.title: Final Report (Part II: A Head-Mounted Three-Dimensional Display), I. E. Sutherland
sources.quote: present the user with a perspective image which changes as he moves

sources.title: The Sword of Damocles (virtual reality)
sources.quote: The system was created in 1968 by computer scientist Ivan Sutherland with the help of his students Bob Sproull

note: Kept the second pass date. Rejected earlier: Heilig's Sensorama (1962 prototype, pre-filmed, not computer-generated), Philco Headsight (1961, camera-fed remote viewing), Sutherland's 1965 'Ultimate Display' (a proposal). The Sutherland system is crude (wireframe), so the fit to 'convincing enough to feel real' is partial; the report says observers remark on the realism of the stereo images.
searched: ia_search3 'head-mounted three dimensional display' 1966-1972; WebSearch for the 1968 FJCC paper; CHM archive report PDF; Wikipedia Sensorama and Sword of Damocles pages.

what: VPL Research's Reality Built for Two (EyePhone head-mounted display plus DataGlove) was sold and in use at outside sites, and W Industries' Virtuality 1000SU VR systems were launched and sold to corporations such as BT, Ford and IBM.
fit: Commercial head-mounted systems that put a user inside a computer-generated, head-tracked 3D world were delivered to paying customers for research, design and training.

sources.title: NASA Tech Briefs, August 1990. Volume 14, No. 8
sources.quote: VPL is now laying the groundwork for a project called RealityNet which will connect the company with RB2 users at the University of North Carolina, MIT

sources.title: Release 1.0 - October, 1990
sources.quote: VPL Research, a leader in the field and the most active vendor, sells trans- ducer hardware and some related software

sources.title: Virtuality (product)
sources.quote: The first two networked VR systems were sold to British Telecom Research Laboratories to experiment with networked telepresence applications.

note: Kept 1990 but with better sources. Earlier candidates: the USAF Super Cockpit / VCASS helmet-mounted display (1980s, research testbed, not a delivered product), UNC GROPE (1971, force feedback only), NASA VIEW (1985-87, research) and VPL's 1989 RB2 public demo (Rheingold, lending book, not readable). The Wikipedia EyePhone page calls the EyePhone 'primarily a research device', so the exact first paid customer use is uncertain; 1990 is when both VPL and W Industries are documented as selling to users. The GamesX issue of 1991-03 reports W Industries' launch in March 1991 of the Virtuality 1000SD.
searched: ia_search3 for 'Reality Built for Two' 1987-1991, VPL Research EyePhone sold 1988-1990, Virtuality arcade 1990-1992; fetched NASA Tech Briefs Aug 1990, Release 1.0 Oct 1990, GamesX Mar 1991, Wikipedia Virtuality and VPL Research.

concept_note: Demonstration (Sutherland 1968) and practical use (1990) kept, with contemporary sources added; practical use now based on both VPL and Virtuality sales in 1990. No mass_adoption: Quest 2 (2020) passed 10 million shipped by Nov 2021, but routine use by ordinary people is still niche, so I give no year.
